Your response was: "Looked at it. Most of it made sense. One thing didn't — two buttons at the bottom. Went to the wrong one first. Darker one drew my eye. That wasn't the action I needed."

We want to understand what you meant by "went to the wrong one first", so let's go a bit deeper. Which of these best captures what you were pointing at?

A) The bottom action area places “Continue Shopping” above “Place Order,” making the upper button appear like the primary next step in the layout.  
B) The “Continue Shopping” button is more visually prominent than “Place Order,” so the hierarchy makes it seem like the main action.  
C) The “Place Order” button is positioned below the more prominent bottom button and near small legal text, making it feel buried in the layout.  
D) None of the above — but only if A, B, and C genuinely miss what you meant (you must still name the specific element you were referring to)

Select A, B, C, or D to continue.

Contrast between the two carries the hierarchy signal. Right now both compete at similar fill weight with the wrong one winning. One CSS pass, two buttons, done.
